title: A railroad legacy, a father’s example, a path of her own
body_markdown:
Four generations of railroaders, one lesson that mattered most: a father's choice to do the right thing and how his daughter is carrying it forward.


**Key takeaways**


- Cappi Seidl is part of a four-generation railroad family that dates to 1929, when her great-grandfather joined the Erie Railroad.
- Her father, retired locomotive engineer Robert “Bob” Woodruff, spent 42 years in the industry and 27 years representing fellow railroaders through the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen.
- Today, she mentors others, especially women in operations, and carries forward her father’s example of doing the right thing.


For Cappi Seidl, a four-generation railroad legacy is about more than a shared profession. Her father, retired locomotive engineer Robert “Bob” Woodruff, taught her to work hard, care for others and do the right thing — lessons that have shaped her career.


“If you’re always doing the right thing for the right reasons, then you’ll be able to look yourself in the mirror,” said Bob.


“He’s absolutely the best role model for me and my brother,” said Cappi. “We’re so lucky to have him and grateful for everything he's done for our family.”


**A legacy dating to 1929**


The family’s railroad history dates to 1929, when Cappi’s great-grandfather, Harry H. Woodruff, joined the Erie Railroad. Her grandfather, Clarence T. Woodruff, continued the tradition, followed by her father, who joined the Erie Lackawanna Railroad in 1968 as a fireman before becoming an engineer.


Although his forefathers were railroaders, Bob knew he wanted to set a better example through his own life and for the children he hoped to have one day. His 42-year career spanned Erie Lackawanna, Conrail and ultimately Norfolk Southern as railroad mergers reshaped the industry. He also spent 27 years representing fellow railroaders through the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen union, serving as a local chairman and later as president.


His union responsibilities often followed him home. As a child, Cappi answered calls from railroaders who needed his help and wrote down their concerns.


“I was kind of like his little secretary,” she recalled. “I would take notes from the guys who had complaints or needed him to follow up on something.”


**Planting a seed**


Cappi did not initially plan to become a railroader. While reevaluating her academic path in college, Bob encouraged her to apply for a train dispatcher position at Norfolk Southern, noting that the tuition assistance program could help support her educational goals.


“I wanted her to have a job where there was stability, where she would be able to make a decent wage and be self-sustaining, not depending on anybody else,” Bob said. “The railroad was a good place to do that because it had done that for me.”


Cappi joined Norfolk Southern as a train dispatcher in 2002, beginning her own chapter in the family’s railroad history.


**Building her own path**


After 11 years as a Pittsburgh dispatcher and about five and a half as chief train dispatcher, she moved to Atlanta when Norfolk Southern consolidated dispatching, becoming an operations superintendent at the Network Operations Center.


She worked in Performance Excellence on the Keystone Division and as an assistant superintendent on the Midwest and Coastal divisions before returning to Network Operations and becoming a director.


Bob helped her understand train handling, mechanical issues, and Collective Bargaining Agreements. During challenging operational periods and demanding work schedules, he encouraged her to remain patient, resilient, and focused on the opportunities ahead.


“He was really helpful in educating me on railroad operations, and why some things take longer than expected,” Cappi said. “He would tell me to stick with it and trust that the hard work would pay off.”


After working with few women early in her career, Cappi values mentoring and supporting other women in operations. “I appreciate having the opportunity to work with more women across the railroad and being part of a support network where we can learn from and encourage one another,” she said. Sharing railroad knowledge with the next generation of women in operations is especially rewarding, she added.


**A legacy that continued beyond retirement**


As Bob approached retirement, Cappi had a chance to experience the railroad beside the father who had encouraged her to join it. Their round trip from Conway to Harrisburg became one of her most cherished memories.


“When my dad was retiring I got to take a trip with him on trains from Conway to Harrisburg and back. It was so cool to see him run an engine and we had a really good time,” Cappi recalled.


After retiring as a locomotive engineer in 2011, Bob worked for about two years as a consultant and instructor at Norfolk Southern’s training center in McDonough, Georgia. The move allowed him to care for his wife while helping test and develop locomotive simulator software to train future engineers.


**Moving the legacy forward**


Today, Cappi carries her father’s lessons into the work of overseeing train movements across Norfolk Southern’s network and mentoring others starting their careers. His example lives on not just in the career she chose, but in how she supports those finding their own way.


Four generations gave Cappi a railroad legacy. Bob showed her that a legacy is not only what you inherit, it is the example you choose to set. By doing the right thing, he changed the course of his family. Now, Cappi carries that example forward.


*By Jihan Gary, Senior Communications Manager*


**


*Jihan Gary leads internal communications for Norfolk Southern, focusing on change management and employee communications. She also oversees strategic communications for Digital and Technology, Human Resources and Compliance. Jihan joined NS in 2023, with over 15 years of corporate communications expertise.*
